summary: A snapshot of the standardization state of Internet protocols as of April 17, 2001, listing the official protocol standards RFCs. It is not a complete index to the RFC series. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 2900.

eli5.summary: A teacher posts a list of which class rules are official on one particular day. Rules change, so the list is old now and a newer list replaced it.

questions: how does the ietf standardization process work
subtitle: The IETF's snapshot of which protocols were standards in 2001.

tldr.problem: The Internet has hundreds of specifications (RFCs). Engineers and operators need to know which protocols are official standards, which are still being tested, which are historical, and what maturity level each has reached.
tldr.mechanism: This document lists every protocol the IETF considers an official Internet Standard, plus those in earlier stages of standardization (Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental) and those that are Historic. It organizes them by maturity level and provides both RFC number and standard number (STD) references, capturing the landscape as of April 17, 2001.
tldr.outcome: This is a periodic snapshot of the standardization landscape at a point in time. It superseded RFC 2700 and was in turn replaced by RFC 2900 as new protocols matured and old ones were replaced.

today: RFC 2800 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 2900 in August 2001. The Internet standards process has continued to evolve, and the IETF no longer publishes periodic snapshots of this form; current standards information is maintained online at the RFC Editor website.

sections.title: What this document is
sections.content:
RFC 2800 is a standards status document published by the IETF in May 2001. It describes the state of standardization of protocols used in the Internet as of April 17, 2001, categorizing each protocol by its maturity level within the standardization process. The document is not a complete index of all RFCs; it lists only those protocols that have gone through (or are going through) the formal IETF standardization process.

This edition supersedes RFC 2700 and was itself replaced by RFC 2900, as the standards landscape continues to evolve.
sections.eli5: This is the IETF's official list of Internet protocols from 2001, organized by how official and tested each one is. It replaced an older list and was later replaced by a newer list as protocols changed.

sections.title: How the standardization process works
sections.content:
The IETF uses a multi-stage process to standardize protocols. When the IETF publishes a new technical specification as an RFC, it starts as a Proposed Standard and must demonstrate widespread interest and engineering consensus. Once it passes review and two independent interoperable implementations exist, it moves to Draft Standard. After additional operational experience, it can become an Internet Standard (the highest level).

The document also lists Experimental RFCs, which are protocols for research or testing that are not on a path to standardization, and Historic RFCs, which are protocols that are no longer used or have been superseded.
sections.eli5: Protocols start as test rules, move to trial status, and eventually become official standards if they work well. If a rule stops being useful, it gets marked as old history.

sections.title: The lists
sections.content:
This document provides lists of protocols organized by standardization level. Standard Protocols are listed both by STD number (a stable reference that persists even if the RFC is updated) and by RFC number. Each entry shows the protocol name, title, RFC number, and STD number (if assigned). Draft Standard and Proposed Standard sections list hundreds of protocols in various stages of development. Experimental and Historic sections list protocols that are not on a path to official standardization.

Asterisks mark protocols that changed status since the previous edition of this document, making it easy to spot what has moved between maturity levels.
sections.eli5: The document is organized like a filing system: official standards here, rules being tested there, old retired rules in another place. Little stars show what moved since the last time the document was published.

sections.title: The living standards list
sections.content:
This RFC documents a snapshot in time, but the IETF points out that an updated list is maintained daily on the RFC Editor web site (www.rfc-editor.org/rfcxx00.html). The snapshot approach was useful for historical reference, showing exactly what was official on a given date.

RFC 2800 was replaced by RFC 2900 in August 2001, which served the same purpose with updated protocol information.
sections.eli5: This list captures the exact state of protocols on one specific day in 2001. While new official lists are published whenever things change enough, this document shows what was official at that particular moment in time.
